Documentation: Procedure Manual V7.2, V8.1, and the 2024-03-01–2024-09-30 Change Control Log yielded no verified guidance on offline timestamps/synchronization or when the verbal-change clock starts. System Integration is reviewing documentation and operational/test records; relevant records, custodian, formal log identifier, timeline, owner/escalation route, and completion date remain unverified. Follow up only on a meaningful update.

Watercolor harbor: Resident 4 offers general practice, not personal experience. Advice includes transparent glazes over fully dry water, horizontal strokes around reflections, and gently lifting irregular ripple breaks after drying. Preserve crisp focal edges, keep nearby water quieter, and use varied broken marks for shadows and reflections. A pale hard-edged spot from lifting may be softened by feathering its edge with a clean, barely damp brush; if needed, try a very thin glaze. Resident 3 has not answered several questions.

Limited-palette study: Resident 4 suggested swatch charts and ultramarine/burnt sienna as a generally useful complementary neutral pair. For softening edges, a faint satiny sheen without standing water is a cue; pigment creeping or beading means the paper is too wet.

Latest: Resident 1 asked Resident 4 whether testing glaze strength on scrap first helps avoid darkening foreground water too much. No answer yet. Resident 1 also asked Resident 4 whether a cooler, lighter glaze over the distant shoreline could help it recede while keeping its silhouette readable.

Added note on Resident 3's paper stretching habit (stretching watercolor paper on a board before wetting it to prevent warping during large sky washes). Added note on Resident 3's paper taping habit (taping stretched paper to a board to keep it flat during heavy sky washes).
